records.name: Bhutan
records.summary:
Bhutan is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2021 — a genuine turning point — and LGBTIQ organisations can now register and operate legally (Pride Bhutan, Rainbow Bhutan). The government engages with UNFPA's Free & Equal campaign at the level of the Royal Court of Justice and Cabinet. Trans women report violence and discrimination remain widespread (trans people 4x more likely to experience assault), and there is no legal gender recognition, but there is no criminalisation, no police targeting pattern, and a monarchy-led culture that discourages open aggression.

Tourism is tightly regulated (daily fee system), which incidentally provides visitors a structured, monitored environment.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021; LGBTIQ organisations can register (though the process is lengthy). No stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit SOGISC protections; legal gender recognition is unavailable in practice, though authorities previously allowed some changes.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service (Nov 2024): 'Trans women face hurdles in reporting violence' - trans people are over four times more likely to experience assault; a 49-year-old trans woman describes having nowhere to report assaults, family pressure to 'accept it as fate', and laws that 'only cater to men and women'.

UNFPA Bhutan report 'Fostering Awareness: Advancing LGBT+ Rights & Inclusivity in Bhutan' (March 2025, 37pp): the 2024 Free & Equal campaign advanced LGBTIQ+ equality among policymakers, parliamentarians and institutions (Royal Court of Justice, Attorney General, Cabinet Secretariat), securing the first direct dialogue between the LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians in Bhutan's history.

Erasing 76 Crimes (June 2019): Bhutan's lower house voted nearly unanimously (43-1) to repeal the 'unnatural sex' provisions (Sections 213-214, punishable by 1 month to 1 year, unenforced for at least 15 years); Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (March 2021): Bhutan's Penal Code Amendment Act came into force Feb 17, 2021 - after the upper house reinserted the provision, a joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex'; decriminalisation completed.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature: 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow' - the emergence of Bhutan's LGBT community via the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page; profiles of administrators and Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly (who fought to wear a kira to school at 16); notes self-stigma is significant but discrimination 'not very widespread'.

The Daily Beast (Oct 2015): 'Gay in Nirvana' - Bhutan's small LGBT population has experienced very little persecution or violence, but the concept of being gay or trans is 'pretty much unheard of'; no shared language for these identities; lesbianism under-recognised; Karma Dupchen created the first public LGBT outlet (LGBT Bhutan Facebook page) in 2013.

freshness.fact: Decriminalisation of 2021 stands (matches cited 76crimes item); unions still unrecognised, gender-marker change permitted; UNFPA overview current. No post-2021 reversal found.

records.name: Botswana
records.summary:
Botswana is workable for trans visitors — Africa's strongest judicial record after South Africa. The High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in 2019 (Letsweletse Motshidiemang v AG, upheld 2021); the Court of Appeal ordered the government to register LEGABIBO; and trans people have won document-change cases (ND v Attorney General, 2017). Draft 2024 constitutional changes even contemplate intersex rights. Implementation lags the rulings (SALC documents unsatisfactory compliance), social conservatism persists, and there is no general LGR statute — but the courts are a genuine protection, unique in the region.

For a visitor: decriminalised, functioning courts, moderate social hostility.

sources.claim: SALC article (May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers: courts in Botswana and Namibia have issued landmark LGBTQI+ rulings (Botswana: LEGABIBO registration ordered 2016; 2019 High Court decriminalisation upheld on appeal 2021), but implementation of the orders has been unsatisfactory - governments slow to comply.
Alta Advisory (June 2024): Botswana's proposed constitutional change would protect intersex rights - analysis of the reform process.

UN UPR outcome report for Botswana (43rd session, May 2023): recommendations to repeal Section 167 of the Penal Code (criminalising same-sex conduct for women) and to introduce a clear administrative process for legal gender recognition did not enjoy Botswana's support; same-sex relations between women remain criminalised and no LGR process exists.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: general human-rights assessment (violence against women, prison conditions, San discrimination) - the LGBT section documents the then-criminalised status and societal discrimination.

LEGABIBO (Lesbians, Gays & Bisexuals of Botswana) official blog: the organisation's activities - World AIDS Day commemorations, HIV stigma work, Pan Africa ILGA conference participation - documenting the community organisation's operations after winning its registration battle.

The Independent (Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time - Tshepo Ricki Kgositau (director of Gender Dynamix) will receive a female ID card after a four-year legal battle; a landmark for trans rights in Botswana.
Human Rights Watch (Jan 2018): 'For LGBT Rights, 2018 Will Be the Year of the Courts' — names Botswana's decriminalisation case among the year's key litigation fronts.

freshness.fact: Sources pre-date the landmark rulings: colonial sodomy laws struck down 11 Jun 2019 (upheld on appeal 29 Nov 2021); trans legal-gender right confirmed 2017-22. Situation improved beyond all five cited documents.

records.name: Central African Republic
records.summary: Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the state barely exists outside Bangui; armed groups control most territory; mob violence and police extortion against perceived LGBT people are documented; no LGR, no community infrastructure.

sources.claim: ILGA World 'Our Identities Under Arrest' (2023) - global report on laws criminalising LGBT people; the fetched copy contained no extractable text at research time (image-based PDF).

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: official assessment including the SOGI section - same-sex conduct not criminalised but societal discrimination and the absence of protections in a conflict-affected state.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture, rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, harsh prison conditions - general human-rights context with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes/ILGA (May 2019): overview of LGBT rights in five Central African countries (Cameroon, CAR, Chad, Gabon, DRC) by activists Julie Makuala Di Baku and Jean Paul Enama - SOGI issues remain taboo and 'contrary to African values'; Cameroon kept its criminalising provision; CAR has a legal vacuum; walking the streets as a same-sex couple is visibly difficult across the region.

UN OHCHR summary of stakeholders' submissions for the CAR's UPR (45th session, Jan 2024): covers international obligations, national human-rights framework, institutional infrastructure - includes SOGI-related stakeholder recommendations.

freshness.fact: Current overview: same-sex acts legal, but public same-sex affection display criminalised — the 2019-2023 'Our Identities Under Arrest' era framing no longer matches; cited State Dept 2023 page superseded by newer code practice.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Central African Republic

records.name: Canada
records.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code's hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveler warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets.

sources.claim: Statistics Canada (March 2026): police-reported hate crime in 2024 was relatively stable (4,882 incidents, +1%) after a 34% jump 2022-2023; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658; overall hate crime has more than doubled since 2018.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 307 redirect loop); the underlying Egale Canada report analyses 2024 hate-crime data affecting 2SLGBTQI people in Canada.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (timeout); the underlying page presents quick stats from the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings.

Egale Canada UPR submission (2012): overview of LGBT human rights in Canada - sexual orientation in the Charter since 1995, marriage equality 2005; but trans protections limited and varying by jurisdiction, with no federal gender-identity discrimination law at the time; identifies gaps against the Yogyakarta Principles.

CBC News (April 2016): P.E.I. moved to make it easier for trans people to change gender on official documents - the Vital Statistics Act amendment requires only a declaration of identified gender plus a doctor's letter, removing the surgery requirement; welcomed by the trans community.

The Globe and Mail (June 2017): Canada's Senate passed Bill C-16 (67-11), prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and expression - framed as Canadian leadership amid global backlash; contrasts with anti-LGBT violence elsewhere.

Ontario Human Rights Commission policy on discrimination because of sexual orientation: the legal context, case law and legislation under the Ontario Human Rights Code (which also covers gender identity and gender expression) - official provincial human-rights framework.

freshness.fact: 2012 UPR shadow-report cited has been overtaken: gender identity/expression added to Criminal Code & CHRA (2017), conversion therapy a crime (2021/22), marriage since 2005. Re-check any 'gap' claims it contained.

records.name: Switzerland
records.summary:
Switzerland is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender recognition has worked by self-declaration since January 2022 — a personal declaration before the civil registrar, with no court or medical requirements (binary male/female only; no non-binary marker). Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2022 (approved by referendum), gender-neutral rape law took effect in 2024, and employers have a legal duty of care toward trans employees. General crime is exceptionally low.

The notable legislative shortcoming — flagged by the ILGA Rainbow Map and by the government's own review — is that the criminal hate-crime and hate-speech provision (Article 261bis) covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. So a person targeted specifically for being trans does not benefit from that aggravation in criminal law, though the protections available through employment and constitutional law are broader. Reported hate crimes against LGBTIQ people have risen about fivefold since 2020 (around six per week, but from a low absolute base of ~309 cases in 2024).

The federal government adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan against LGBTIQ hate crime in January 2026 (running to 2030), signalling a pro-trans institutional direction. There is no rollback movement.

sources.claim: Swiss Federal Office for Gender Equality official page: since 1 July 2020, public incitement to hatred/discrimination based on sexual orientation is punishable (Art. 261bis Criminal Code); 'Marriage for All' in force since 1 July 2022; covers LGBTIQ rights developments.

EPFL page on gender identity in the Swiss civil status register: since 1 January 2022, any person registered in a Swiss municipality may change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar - no court or medical requirement; changes are generally limited to binary categories, with some cantonal variation.
Swissinfo: hundreds of people in Switzerland have changed their legal gender using the simplified self-declaration process introduced in 2022.
Swissinfo: Switzerland records roughly six hate crimes per week against LGBTIQ people (based on monitoring reports).

Swiss Federal Office for Gender Equality: on 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted the first National Action Plan to combat hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030, with three pillars - victim support and protection, prevention, and monitoring of violence.
Swissinfo coverage of the same first national action plan against anti-LGBTIQ hate crimes (2026).

LegalClarity overview (June 2026): marriage equality since July 2022 (64.1% referendum approval); criminal-law protection against sexual-orientation discrimination since 2020; streamlined legal gender change since January 2022. Notes gaps: gender identity is not fully covered by the criminal anti-discrimination provision, and conversion therapy and surrogacy remain unregulated.

trans welcome platform (Swiss): the legal framework for trans people at work - employers' duty of care under Art. 328 OR and the Equality Act (GLG); employees may use their preferred name and gender at work without official change; employers must keep trans identity confidential; solutions for showers/toilets/cloakrooms must respect everyone's personal rights; the trans person may wear service clothing matching their gender identity.
ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Switzerland: overall index score and per-category compliance breakdown (after the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes).

OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report for Switzerland: Switzerland regularly reports hate-crime data; the Criminal Code has no general hate-crime provision - hate crimes are addressed under anti-discrimination provisions (Art. 261bis); ODIHR notes recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes and police do not record bias motivation.

UNHCR Switzerland page: everyone in Switzerland has the right to equal treatment; discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited; LGBTIQ+ people enjoy equal rights; same-sex couples can marry since 1 July 2022; lists reporting mechanisms and support organisations.

freshness.fact: Marriage/adoption/IVF in force 1 Jul 2022 (64% referendum); acts legal since 1942, equal consent since 1992; the two cited official pages (EBG rights overview, civil-registry explainer) are living documents aligned with current law.

records.name: Chile
records.summary:
Chile has a strong legal framework — a gender identity law allowing self-determination (2019, no medical requirements), marriage equality (2022), a hate-crime law covering gender identity (2012), and a positive Gendarmería protocol that places trans inmates in facilities matching their gender identity and provides healthcare examination (better than most European countries on axis-H). The UN Human Rights Committee commended Chile's police measures to promote LGBTIQ rights.

But 2024 was a "year of regression" (the first rollback since democracy returned in 1990), with lawmakers rejecting nondiscrimination-law reforms and a 2025 Movilh report describing a "breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus" on LGBTIQ+ rights. Documented violence includes a trans person murdered and dismembered ("the biggest hate crime in Chile"), a transphobic hotel attack in Santiago (beating, captivity, death threats), and institutional discrimination against Chile's first trans police officer.

The Supreme Court restored a femicide conviction for the murder of a trans woman (overturning an appeals-court ruling that she didn't "legally qualify" as a woman). For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms unrestricted, Santiago is welcoming.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; hate-crime law includes SOGI as aggravating circumstances since 2012; civil unions since 2015; comprehensive self-determination-based legal gender recognition law passed 2019; third sex option for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006; non-binding intersex-affirming health guidance (2023) recommends against unnecessary surgeries; in 2025 a court issued Chile's first lesbophobic femicide conviction.
Washington Blade (Mar 2025): '2024 was a 'year of regression' for LGBTQ rights in Chile' — annual rights report finds setbacks for equality and trans rights, including stalled legislation.
NOTE: The MOVILH (Chilean LGBT integration movement) 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity (2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

BioBioChile investigation (Jan 2024, in Spanish): profile of Ever, a young trans man murdered and dismembered in 2023 - described as Chile's 'biggest hate crime'; the killer, an acquaintance, confessed.

Chilevisión (Sept 2021, in Spanish): a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a Santiago hotel in a transphobic attack; victim recounts fearing for his life.

La Tercera (in Spanish): Chile's prison service (Gendarmería) signed a new protocol for trans inmates - placement according to gender identity, segmented housing, medical examination on entry to determine hormonal/surgical treatment needs, and respect for assumed-gender expression.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile: composite scores measuring LGBT rights perception, including a specific Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

El Universal Chile (April 2025, in Spanish): Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros for discrimination - relegated to administrative tasks, private life exposed without consent, denied support against online hate, and transition-related surgery refused.

Movilh (Chilean LGBT integration movement) achievements page: lists the organisation's historical milestones across legal, judicial, public-policy, human-rights, mobilisation and international sectors benefiting lesbians, gays, bisexuals and trans people in Chile - institutional-culture context.

records.name: China
records.summary:
China demands real caution — authoritarian but not criminalising. The most directly visitor-specific finding is airport discrimination: a Thai trans YouTuber was singled out and subjected to discriminatory treatment at a Chinese airport. The most severe documented case is forced psychiatric commitment: a trans woman was held for 97 days and subjected to electroshock "conversion" therapy under family pressure (she won unprecedented compensation), showing the medical/psychiatric system can be weaponized — though this targeted a resident, not a tourist.

Under Xi Jinping, the space for LGBTQ+ organising and expression is shrinking: Pride-month social-media and film censorship, a government crackdown on LGBT NGOs (2023), a performance ban on transgender TV icon Jin Xing, and cancellation of a foreign drag queen's tour. There is no criminalisation of trans identity, no bathroom restriction law, and courts can provide some protection, but there are no anti-discrimination protections.

China is a regional gender-affirming-care hub, but the parental-consent barrier applies even to adults.

sources.claim: The Thaiger (May 2025): renowned Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong accused Chinese immigration officers of sexist, mocking treatment during a family trip - officers laughed at and questioned her at a Chinese airport. Directly relevant to trans travellers' airport experiences in China.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT investigation (Dec 2024) covers transgender 'conversion' practices in China.

The Guardian (Nov 2024): performance artist Ling'er, 28, won a record payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment - the first time a trans person won such a case in China; she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights.
Human Rights Watch (Jun 2026): 'China: Social Media, Films Censored Around Pride Month' — platforms scrubbed LGBT-related posts and films around Pride month in a renewed censorship wave.

Radio Free Asia (Jan 2024): the CCP continues a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people as part of a campaign against 'foreign ideologies' - public display of rainbow flags banned, activism 'all but extinct' on the mainland, in contrast to Taiwan's 2019 marriage equality; queer and trans people report growing abuse.

Foreign Policy (Jan 2025): 'Trans People in China Face Barriers to Gender-Affirming Care' — gender transition is treated as 'a family affair': surgery requires parental consent and family involvement, and new rules restrict access.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): China's approach is 'don't encourage, don't oppose, don't promote', but increasingly restrictive - the Cybersecurity Law enables censorship of LGBTIQ content; in 2025 several gay dating apps were removed from the Apple App Store and prominent queer accounts forced to rebrand or shut down; most advocacy organisations have closed or gone underground; narrow 'family values' pressure intensifies.

CNN (Jan 2025): 'Some in China fear a wider LGBTQ+ crackdown after transgender dancer Jin Xing's shows canceled' — the cancellation of the famous transgender TV personality's tour fuels fears of a broader clampdown.
Swissinfo: a Swiss drag queen faces Chinese repression - reporting on the treatment of a gender-nonconforming performer in China.
CNN (Mar 2016): 'China bans same-sex romance from TV screens' — broadcast regulator SAPPRFT guidelines bar depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour' including same-sex romance.

records.name: Côte d'Ivoire
records.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp recent deterioration. Long considered West Africa's tolerant outlier (same-sex conduct has never been criminalised), the country saw a wave of violence in late 2024: social-media influencers exhorted followers to “hunt” gay and gender-nonconforming people, and dozens of assaults and beatings followed (NYT, Oct 2024). There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection; police response to the hunt wave was inadequate.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but the 2024 hunt-down campaign makes visible gender nonconformity dangerous, especially in Abidjan.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying NYT article (Oct 2024) covers the situation of LGBTQ people in Ivory Coast (Côte d'Ivoire).

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation/prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: official assessment including the SOGI section - same-sex conduct not criminalised but societal discrimination, and the significant violence against LGBT persons documented in the report period.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Academic article (Critical African Studies, 2015) by Matthew Thomann and Robbie Corey-Boulet: 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis' - travestis (people born male living as women full- or part-time) in Côte d'Ivoire encounter harsher stigmatisation than other sexual/gender minorities; documents violence, exclusion and community resilience.
Same article as above (PMC canonical URL): 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis' - the key academic source on trans-feminine people's experiences in Côte d'Ivoire.

freshness.fact: Current overview describes same-sex activity as legal for both sexes (no specific protections, unrecognised unions); the 'acts against nature'/public-indecency provisions in the cited 2023-era reports no longer appear — recheck criminalisation claims.
